For right-censored data, if a censored observation has the same value as an uncensored one, the uncensored observation should be placed first. For left-censored data, if a censored observation has the same value as an uncensored one, the censored observation should be placed first.

Note that in this case the quantity x(i)x_{(i)} does not necessarily represent the ii’th “largest” observation from the (unknown) complete sample.

Finally, let Ω\Omega (omega) denote the set of nn subscripts in the “ordered” sample that correspond to uncensored observations.

Estimation

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (method="mle")
For Type I left censored data, the likelihood function is given by:

L(μ,τ|x_)=(Nc1c2…ckn)∏j=1k[F(Tj)]cj∏i∈Ωf[x(i)](7) L(\mu, \tau | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c_1 c_2 \ldots c_k n} \prod_{j=1}^k [F(T_j)]^{c_j} \prod_{i \in \Omega} f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (7)

where ff and FF denote the probability density function (pdf) and cumulative distribution function (cdf) of the population (Cohen, 1963; Cohen, 1991, pp.6, 50). That is,

f(t)=tκ−1e−t/θθκΓ(κ)(8) f(t) = \frac{t^{\kappa-1} e^{-t/\theta}}{\theta^\kappa \Gamma(\kappa)} \;\;\;\;\;\; (8)

(Johnson et al., 1994, p.343), where κ\kappa and θ\theta are defined in terms of μ\mu and τ\tau by Equations (1) and (2) above.

For left singly censored data, Equation (7) simplifies to:

L(μ,τ|x_)=(Nc)[F(T)]c∏i=c+1nf[x(i)](9) L(\mu, \tau | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c} [F(T)]^{c} \prod_{i = c+1}^n f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (9)

Similarly, for Type I right censored data, the likelihood function is given by:

L(μ,τ|x_)=(Nc1c2…ckn)∏j=1k[1−F(Tj)]cj∏i∈Ωf[x(i)](10) L(\mu, \tau | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c_1 c_2 \ldots c_k n} \prod_{j=1}^k [1 - F(T_j)]^{c_j} \prod_{i \in \Omega} f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (10)

and for right singly censored data this simplifies to:

L(κ,θ|x_)=(Nc)[1−F(T)]c∏i=1nf[x(i)](11) L(\kappa, \theta | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c} [1 - F(T)]^{c} \prod_{i = 1}^n f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (11)

The maximum likelihood estimators are computed by minimizing the negative log-likelihood function.

Confidence Intervals
This section explains how confidence intervals for the mean μ\mu are computed.

Likelihood Profile (ci.method="profile.likelihood")
This method was proposed by Cox (1970, p.88), and Venzon and Moolgavkar (1988) introduced an efficient method of computation. This method is also discussed by Stryhn and Christensen (2003) and Royston (2007). The idea behind this method is to invert the likelihood-ratio test to obtain a confidence interval for the mean μ\mu while treating the coefficient of variation τ\tau as a nuisance parameter. Equation (7) above shows the form of the likelihood function L(μ,τ|x_)L(\mu, \tau | \underline{x}) for multiply left-censored data, where μ\mu and τ\tau are defined by Equations (3) and (4), and Equation (10) shows the function for multiply right-censored data.

Following Stryhn and Christensen (2003), denote the maximum likelihood estimates of the mean and coefficient of variation by (μ*,τ*)(\mu^*, \tau^*). The likelihood ratio test statistic (G2G^2) of the hypothesis H0:μ=μ0H_0: \mu = \mu_0 (where μ0\mu_0 is a fixed value) equals the drop in 2log(L)2 log(L) between the “full” model and the reduced model with μ\mu fixed at μ0\mu_0, i.e.,

G2=2{log[L(μ*,τ*)]−log[L(μ0,τ0*)]}(12) G^2 = 2 \{log[L(\mu^*, \tau^*)] - log[L(\mu_0, \tau_0^*)]\} \;\;\;\;\;\; (12)

where τ0*\tau_0^* is the maximum likelihood estimate of τ\tau for the reduced model (i.e., when μ=μ0\mu = \mu_0). Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic G2G^2 follows a chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom.

Alternatively, we may express the test statistic in terms of the profile likelihood function L1L_1 for the mean μ\mu, which is obtained from the usual likelihood function by maximizing over the parameter τ\tau, i.e.,

L1(μ)=maxτL(μ,τ)(13) L_1(\mu) = max_{\tau} L(\mu, \tau) \;\;\;\;\;\; (13)

Then we have

G2=2{log[L1(μ*)]−log[L1(μ0)]}(14) G^2 = 2 \{log[L_1(\mu^*)] - log[L_1(\mu_0)]\} \;\;\;\;\;\; (14)

A two-sided (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence interval for the mean μ\mu consists of all values of μ0\mu_0 for which the test is not significant at level alphaalpha:

μ0:G2≤χ1,1−α2(15) \mu_0: G^2 \le \chi^2_{1, {1-\alpha}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (15)

where χν,p2\chi^2_{\nu, p} denotes the pp’th quantile of the chi-squared distribution with ν\nu degrees of freedom. One-sided lower and one-sided upper confidence intervals are computed in a similar fashion, except that the quantity 1−α1-\alpha in Equation (15) is replaced with 1−2α1-2\alpha.

Normal Approximation (ci.method="normal.approx")
This method constructs approximate (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence intervals for μ\mu based on the assumption that the estimator of μ\mu is approximately normally distributed. That is, a two-sided (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence interval for μ\mu is constructed as:

[μ̂−t1−α/2,m−1σ̂μ̂,μ̂+t1−α/2,m−1σ̂μ̂](16) [\hat{\mu} - t_{1-\alpha/2, m-1}\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\mu}}, \; \hat{\mu} + t_{1-\alpha/2, m-1}\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\mu}}] \;\;\;\; (16)

where μ̂\hat{\mu} denotes the estimate of μ\mu, σ̂μ̂\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\mu}} denotes the estimated asymptotic standard deviation of the estimator of μ\mu, mm denotes the assumed sample size for the confidence interval, and tp,νt_{p,\nu} denotes the pp’th quantile of Student’s t-distribuiton with ν\nu degrees of freedom. One-sided confidence intervals are computed in a similar fashion.

The argument ci.sample.size determines the value of mm and by default is equal to the number of uncensored observations. This is simply an ad-hoc method of constructing confidence intervals and is not based on any published theoretical results.

When pivot.statistic="z", the pp’th quantile from the standard normal distribution is used in place of the pp’th quantile from Student’s t-distribution.

The standard deviation of the mle of μ\mu is estimated based on the inverse of the Fisher Information matrix.

Bootstrap and Bias-Corrected Bootstrap Approximation (ci.method="bootstrap")
The bootstrap is a nonparametric method of estimating the distribution (and associated distribution parameters and quantiles) of a sample statistic, regardless of the distribution of the population from which the sample was drawn. The bootstrap was introduced by Efron (1979) and a general reference is Efron and Tibshirani (1993).

In the context of deriving an approximate (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence interval for the population mean μ\mu, the bootstrap can be broken down into the following steps:

  1. Create a bootstrap sample by taking a random sample of size NN from the observations in x_\underline{x}, where sampling is done with replacement. Note that because sampling is done with replacement, the same element of x_\underline{x} can appear more than once in the bootstrap sample. Thus, the bootstrap sample will usually not look exactly like the original sample (e.g., the number of censored observations in the bootstrap sample will often differ from the number of censored observations in the original sample).
  2. Estimate μ\mu based on the bootstrap sample created in Step 1, using the same method that was used to estimate μ\mu using the original observations in x_\underline{x}. Because the bootstrap sample usually does not match the original sample, the estimate of μ\mu based on the bootstrap sample will usually differ from the original estimate based on x_\underline{x}.
  3. Repeat Steps 1 and 2 BB times, where BB is some large number. For the function
    egammaAltCensored, the number of bootstraps BB is determined by the argument n.bootstraps (see the arguments in the egammaAltCensored help page). The default value of n.bootstraps is 1000.
  4. Use the BB estimated values of μ\mu to compute the empirical cumulative distribution function of this estimator of μ\mu (see ecdfPlot), and then create a confidence interval for μ\mu based on this estimated cdf.

The two-sided percentile interval (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993, p.170) is computed as:

[Ĝ−1(α2),Ĝ−1(1−α2)](17) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\frac{\alpha}{2}), \; \hat{G}^{-1}(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})] \;\;\;\;\;\; (17)

where Ĝ(t)\hat{G}(t) denotes the empirical cdf evaluated at tt and thus Ĝ−1(p)\hat{G}^{-1}(p) denotes the pp’th empirical quantile, that is, the pp’th quantile associated with the empirical cdf. Similarly, a one-sided lower confidence interval is computed as:

[Ĝ−1(α),∞](18) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha), \; \infty] \;\;\;\;\;\; (18)

and a one-sided upper confidence interval is computed as:

[0,Ĝ−1(1−α)](19) [0, \; \hat{G}^{-1}(1-\alpha)] \;\;\;\;\;\; (19)

The function egammaAltCensored calls the R function quantile to compute the empirical quantiles used in Equations (17)-(19).

The percentile method bootstrap confidence interval is only first-order accurate (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993, pp.187-188), meaning that the probability that the confidence interval will contain the true value of μ\mu can be off by k/Nk/\sqrt{N}, where kkis some constant. Efron and Tibshirani (1993, pp.184-188) proposed a bias-corrected and accelerated interval that is second-order accurate, meaning that the probability that the confidence interval will contain the true value of μ\mu may be off by k/Nk/N instead of k/Nk/\sqrt{N}. The two-sided bias-corrected and accelerated confidence interval is computed as:

[Ĝ−1(α1),Ĝ−1(α2)](20) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_1), \; \hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_2)] \;\;\;\;\;\; (20)

where

α1=Φ[ẑ0+ẑ0+zα/21−â(z0+zα/2)](21) \alpha_1 = \Phi[\hat{z}_0 + \frac{\hat{z}_0 + z_{\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat{a}(z_0 + z_{\alpha/2})}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (21)

α2=Φ[ẑ0+ẑ0+z1−α/21−â(z0+z1−α/2)](22) \alpha_2 = \Phi[\hat{z}_0 + \frac{\hat{z}_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat{a}(z_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2})}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (22)

ẑ0=Φ−1[Ĝ(μ̂)](23) \hat{z}_0 = \Phi^{-1}[\hat{G}(\hat{\mu})] \;\;\;\;\;\; (23)

â=∑i=1N(μ̂(⋅)−μ̂(i))36[∑i=1N(μ̂(⋅)−μ̂(i))2]3/2(24) \hat{a} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{\mu}_{(\cdot)} - \hat{\mu}_{(i)})^3}{6[\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{\mu}_{(\cdot)} - \hat{\mu}_{(i)})^2]^{3/2}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (24)

where the quantity μ̂(i)\hat{\mu}_{(i)} denotes the estimate of μ\mu using all the values in x_\underline{x} except the ii’th one, and

μ̂(⋅)=1N∑i=1Nμ(i)̂(25) \hat{\mu}{(\cdot)} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \hat{\mu_{(i)}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (25)

A one-sided lower confidence interval is given by:

[Ĝ−1(α1),∞](26) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_1), \; \infty] \;\;\;\;\;\; (26)

and a one-sided upper confidence interval is given by:

[0,Ĝ−1(α2)](27) [0, \; \hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_2)] \;\;\;\;\;\; (27)

where α1\alpha_1 and α2\alpha_2 are computed as for a two-sided confidence interval, except α/2\alpha/2 is replaced with α\alpha in Equations (21) and (22).

The constant ẑ0\hat{z}_0 incorporates the bias correction, and the constant â\hat{a} is the acceleration constant. The term “acceleration” refers to the rate of change of the standard error of the estimate of μ\mu with respect to the true value of μ\mu (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993, p.186). epoisCensored

Help topic: epoisCensored.

If x or censored contain any missing (NA), undefined (NaN) or infinite (Inf, -Inf) values, they will be removed prior to performing the estimation.

Let x_\underline{x} denote a vector of NN observations from a Poisson distribution with mean lambda=λ\lambda.

Assume nn (0<n<N0 < n < N) of these observations are known and cc (c=N−nc=N-n) of these observations are all censored below (left-censored) or all censored above (right-censored) at kk fixed censoring levels

T1,T2,…,Tk;k≥1(1) T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_k; \; k \ge 1 \;\;\;\;\;\; (1)

For the case when k≥2k \ge 2, the data are said to be Type I multiply censored. For the case when k=1k=1, set T=T1T = T_1. If the data are left-censored and all nn known observations are greater than or equal to TT, or if the data are right-censored and all nn known observations are less than or equal to TT, then the data are said to be Type I singly censored (Nelson, 1982, p.7), otherwise they are considered to be Type I multiply censored.

Let cjc_j denote the number of observations censored below or above censoring level TjT_j for j=1,2,…,kj = 1, 2, \ldots, k, so that

∑i=1kcj=c(2) \sum_{i=1}^k c_j = c \;\;\;\;\;\; (2)

Let x(1),x(2),…,x(N)x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(N)} denote the “ordered” observations, where now “observation” means either the actual observation (for uncensored observations) or the censoring level (for censored observations). For right-censored data, if a censored observation has the same value as an uncensored one, the uncensored observation should be placed first. For left-censored data, if a censored observation has the same value as an uncensored one, the censored observation should be placed first.

Note that in this case the quantity x(i)x_{(i)} does not necessarily represent the ii’th “largest” observation from the (unknown) complete sample.

Finally, let Ω\Omega (omega) denote the set of nn subscripts in the “ordered” sample that correspond to uncensored observations.

Estimation

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (method="mle")
For Type I left censored data, the likelihood function is given by:

L(λ|x_)=(Nc1c2…ckn)∏j=1k[F(Tj)]cj∏i∈Ωf[x(i)](3) L(\lambda | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c_1 c_2 \ldots c_k n} \prod_{j=1}^k [F(T_j)]^{c_j} \prod_{i \in \Omega} f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (3)

where ff and FF denote the probability density function (pdf) and cumulative distribution function (cdf) of the population (Cohen, 1963; Cohen, 1991, pp.6, 50). That is,

f(t)=e−λλtt!,x=0,1,2,…(4) f(t) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^t}{t!}, \; x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \;\;\;\;\;\; (4)

F(t)=∑i=0tf(i)=∑i=0te−λλii!(5) F(t) = \sum_{i=0}^t f(i) = \sum_{i=0}^t \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^i}{i!} \;\;\;\;\;\; (5)

(Johnson et al., 1992, p.151). For left singly censored data, equation (3) simplifies to:

L(λ|x_)=(Nc)[F(T)]c∏i=c+1nf[x(i)](6) L(\lambda | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c} [F(T)]^{c} \prod_{i = c+1}^n f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (6)

Similarly, for Type I right censored data, the likelihood function is given by:

L(λ|x_)=(Nc1c2…ckn)∏j=1k[1−F(Tj)]cj∏i∈Ωf[x(i)](7) L(\lambda | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c_1 c_2 \ldots c_k n} \prod_{j=1}^k [1 - F(T_j)]^{c_j} \prod_{i \in \Omega} f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (7)

and for right singly censored data this simplifies to:

L(λ|x_)=(Nc)[1−F(T)]c∏i=1nf[x(i)](8) L(\lambda | \underline{x}) = {N \choose c} [1 - F(T)]^{c} \prod_{i = 1}^n f[x_{(i)}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (8)

The maximum likelihood estimators are computed by maximizing the likelihood function. For right-censored data, taking the derivative of the log-likelihood function with respect to λ\lambda and setting this to 0 produces the following equation:

x‾=λ{1−∑j=1Kcjn[f(Tj)1−F(Tj)]}(9) \bar{x} = \lambda \{1 - \sum_{j=1}^K \frac{c_j}{n} [\frac{f(T_j)}{1-F(T_j)}] \} \;\;\;\;\;\; (9)

where

x‾=1n∑i∈Ωxi(10) \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i \in \Omega} x_i \;\;\;\;\;\; (10)

Note that the quantity defined in equation (10) is simply the mean of the uncensored observations.

For left-censored data, taking the derivative of the log-likelihood function with respect to λ\lambda and setting this to 0 produces the following equation:

x‾=λ{1+∑j=1Kcjn[f(Tj−1)F(Tj−1)]}(11) \bar{x} = \lambda \{1 + \sum_{j=1}^K \frac{c_j}{n} [\frac{f(T_j - 1)}{F(T_j - 1)}] \} \;\;\;\;\;\; (11)

The function epoisCensored computes the maximum likelihood estimator of λ\lambda by solving Equation (9) (right-censored data) or Equation (11) (left-censored data); it uses the sample mean of the uncensored observations as the initial value.

Setting Censored Observations to Half the Censoring Level (method="half.cen.level")
This method is applicable only to left censored data. This method involves simply replacing all the censored observations with half their detection limit, and then computing the mean and standard deviation with the usual formulas (see epois).

This method is included only to allow comparison of this method to other methods. Setting left-censored observations to half the censoring level is not recommended.

Confidence Intervals
This section explains how confidence intervals for the mean λ\lambda are computed.

Likelihood Profile (ci.method="profile.likelihood")
This method was proposed by Cox (1970, p.88), and Venzon and Moolgavkar (1988) introduced an efficient method of computation. This method is also discussed by Stryhn and Christensen (2003) and Royston (2007). The idea behind this method is to invert the likelihood-ratio test to obtain a confidence interval for the mean λ\lambda. Equation (3) above shows the form of the likelihood function L(λ|x_)L(\lambda | \underline{x}) for multiply left-censored data, and Equation (7) shows the function for multiply right-censored data.

Following Stryhn and Christensen (2003), denote the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean by λ*\lambda^*. The likelihood ratio test statistic (G2G^2) of the hypothesis H0:λ=λ0H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0 (where λ0\lambda_0 is a fixed value) equals the drop in 2log(L)2 log(L) between the “full” model and the reduced model with λ\lambda fixed at μ0\mu_0, i.e.,

G2=2{log[L(λ*)]−log[L(λ0)]}(11) G^2 = 2 \{log[L(\lambda^*)] - log[L(\lambda_0)]\} \;\;\;\;\;\; (11)

. Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic G2G^2 follows a chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom.

A two-sided (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence interval for the mean λ\lambda consists of all values of λ0\lambda_0 for which the test is not significant at level alphaalpha:

λ0:G2≤χ1,1−α2(12) \lambda_0: G^2 \le \chi^2_{1, {1-\alpha}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (12)

where χν,p2\chi^2_{\nu, p} denotes the pp’th quantile of the chi-squared distribution with ν\nu degrees of freedom. One-sided lower and one-sided upper confidence intervals are computed in a similar fashion, except that the quantity 1−α1-\alpha in Equation (12) is replaced with 1−2α1-2\alpha.

Normal Approximation (ci.method="normal.approx")
This method constructs approximate (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence intervals for λ\lambda based on the assumption that the estimator of λ\lambda is approximately normally distributed. That is, a two-sided (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence interval for λ\lambda is constructed as:

[λ̂−t1−α/2,m−1σ̂λ̂,λ̂+t1−α/2,m−1σ̂λ̂](13) [\hat{\lambda} - t_{1-\alpha/2, m-1}\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\lambda}}, \; \hat{\lambda} + t_{1-\alpha/2, m-1}\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\lambda}}] \;\;\;\; (13)

where λ̂\hat{\lambda} denotes the estimate of λ\lambda, σ̂λ̂\hat{\sigma}_{\hat{\lambda}} denotes the estimated asymptotic standard deviation of the estimator of λ\lambda, mm denotes the assumed sample size for the confidence interval, and tp,νt_{p,\nu} denotes the pp’th quantile of Student’s t-distribuiton with ν\nu degrees of freedom. One-sided confidence intervals are computed in a similar fashion.

The argument ci.sample.size determines the value of mm and by default is equal to the number of uncensored observations. This is simply an ad-hoc method of constructing confidence intervals and is not based on any published theoretical results.

When pivot.statistic="z", the pp’th quantile from the standard normal distribution is used in place of the pp’th quantile from Student’s t-distribution.

When λ\lambda is estimated with the maximum likelihood estimator (method="mle"), the variance of λ̂\hat{\lambda} is estimated based on the inverse of the Fisher Information matrix. When λ\lambda is estimated using the half-censoring-level method (method="half.cen.level"), the variance of λ̂\hat{\lambda} is estimated as:

σ̂λ̂2=λ̂m(14) \hat{\sigma}^2_{\hat{\lambda}} = \frac{\hat{\lambda}}{m} \;\;\;\;\;\; (14)

where mm denotes the assumed sample size (see above).

Bootstrap and Bias-Corrected Bootstrap Approximation (ci.method="bootstrap")
The bootstrap is a nonparametric method of estimating the distribution (and associated distribution parameters and quantiles) of a sample statistic, regardless of the distribution of the population from which the sample was drawn. The bootstrap was introduced by Efron (1979) and a general reference is Efron and Tibshirani (1993).

In the context of deriving an approximate (1−α)100%(1-\alpha)100\% confidence interval for the population mean λ\lambda, the bootstrap can be broken down into the following steps:

  1. Create a bootstrap sample by taking a random sample of size NN from the observations in x_\underline{x}, where sampling is done with replacement. Note that because sampling is done with replacement, the same element of x_\underline{x} can appear more than once in the bootstrap sample. Thus, the bootstrap sample will usually not look exactly like the original sample (e.g., the number of censored observations in the bootstrap sample will often differ from the number of censored observations in the original sample).
  2. Estimate λ\lambda based on the bootstrap sample created in Step 1, using the same method that was used to estimate λ\lambda using the original observations in x_\underline{x}. Because the bootstrap sample usually does not match the original sample, the estimate of λ\lambda based on the bootstrap sample will usually differ from the original estimate based on x_\underline{x}.
  3. Repeat Steps 1 and 2 BB times, where BB is some large number. For the function epoisCensored, the number of bootstraps BB is determined by the argument n.bootstraps (see the arguments in the epoisCensored help page). The default value of n.bootstraps is 1000.
  4. Use the BB estimated values of λ\lambda to compute the empirical cumulative distribution function of this estimator of λ\lambda (see ecdfPlot), and then create a confidence interval for λ\lambda based on this estimated cdf.

The two-sided percentile interval (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993, p.170) is computed as:

[Ĝ−1(α2),Ĝ−1(1−α2)](15) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\frac{\alpha}{2}), \; \hat{G}^{-1}(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})] \;\;\;\;\;\; (15)

where Ĝ(t)\hat{G}(t) denotes the empirical cdf evaluated at tt and thus Ĝ−1(p)\hat{G}^{-1}(p) denotes the pp’th empirical quantile, that is, the pp’th quantile associated with the empirical cdf. Similarly, a one-sided lower confidence interval is computed as:

[Ĝ−1(α),∞](16) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha), \; \infty] \;\;\;\;\;\; (16)

and a one-sided upper confidence interval is computed as:

[0,Ĝ−1(1−α)](17) [0, \; \hat{G}^{-1}(1-\alpha)] \;\;\;\;\;\; (17)

The function epoisCensored calls the R function quantile to compute the empirical quantiles used in Equations (15)-(17).

The percentile method bootstrap confidence interval is only first-order accurate (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993, pp.187-188), meaning that the probability that the confidence interval will contain the true value of λ\lambda can be off by k/Nk/\sqrt{N}, where kkis some constant. Efron and Tibshirani (1993, pp.184-188) proposed a bias-corrected and accelerated interval that is second-order accurate, meaning that the probability that the confidence interval will contain the true value of λ\lambda may be off by k/Nk/N instead of k/Nk/\sqrt{N}. The two-sided bias-corrected and accelerated confidence interval is computed as:

[Ĝ−1(α1),Ĝ−1(α2)](18) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_1), \; \hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_2)] \;\;\;\;\;\; (18)

where

α1=Φ[ẑ0+ẑ0+zα/21−â(z0+zα/2)](19) \alpha_1 = \Phi[\hat{z}_0 + \frac{\hat{z}_0 + z_{\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat{a}(z_0 + z_{\alpha/2})}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (19)

α2=Φ[ẑ0+ẑ0+z1−α/21−â(z0+z1−α/2)](20) \alpha_2 = \Phi[\hat{z}_0 + \frac{\hat{z}_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat{a}(z_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2})}] \;\;\;\;\;\; (20)

ẑ0=Φ−1[Ĝ(λ̂)](21) \hat{z}_0 = \Phi^{-1}[\hat{G}(\hat{\lambda})] \;\;\;\;\;\; (21)

â=∑i=1N(λ̂(⋅)−λ̂(i))36[∑i=1N(λ̂(⋅)−λ̂(i))2]3/2(22) \hat{a} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{\lambda}_{(\cdot)} - \hat{\lambda}_{(i)})^3}{6[\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{\lambda}_{(\cdot)} - \hat{\lambda}_{(i)})^2]^{3/2}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (22)

where the quantity λ̂(i)\hat{\lambda}_{(i)} denotes the estimate of λ\lambda using all the values in x_\underline{x} except the ii’th one, and

λ̂(⋅)=1N∑i=1Nλ(i)̂(23) \hat{\lambda}{(\cdot)} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \hat{\lambda_{(i)}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (23)

A one-sided lower confidence interval is given by:

[Ĝ−1(α1),∞](24) [\hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_1), \; \infty] \;\;\;\;\;\; (24)

and a one-sided upper confidence interval is given by:

[0,Ĝ−1(α2)](25) [0, \; \hat{G}^{-1}(\alpha_2)] \;\;\;\;\;\; (25)

where α1\alpha_1 and α2\alpha_2 are computed as for a two-sided confidence interval, except α/2\alpha/2 is replaced with α\alpha in Equations (19) and (20).

The constant ẑ0\hat{z}_0 incorporates the bias correction, and the constant â\hat{a} is the acceleration constant. The term “acceleration” refers to the rate of change of the standard error of the estimate of λ\lambda with respect to the true value of λ\lambda (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993, p.186). For a normal (Gaussian) distribution, the standard error of the estimate of λ\lambda does not depend on the value of λ\lambda, hence the acceleration constant is not really necessary.

When ci.method="bootstrap", the function epoisCensored computes both the percentile method and bias-corrected and accelerated method bootstrap confidence intervals.
